title: How a plant runs itself
question: How does a plant that cannot move feed, defend and organize itself?
hook: A houseplant makes its own food, defends itself with chemicals and sends signals across its body without moving an inch.
idea: A plant stays alive through chemistry, cells and organs that each do a specialised job and signal one another.

beats.prompt: Roots collect minerals and leaves make nutrients. If nothing could carry materials between them, what would happen?

choices.label: Neither organ could stay alive, each missing what the other supplies
The leaves would live on, while the roots grew longer
choices.feedback: It tempts because leaves make nutrients, but the roots need those nutrients to stay alive.

choices.label: Both would be fine, since each makes all it needs
choices.feedback: Roots acquire minerals and leaves manufacture nutrients, so each depends on the other's product.

beats.explain: For both organs to remain living, minerals must be transported to the leaves and manufactured nutrients to the roots.

beats.prompt: match each plant part or feature to its job
pairs: Anchor the plant and acquire minerals
Lets plants make their own nutrients using light
Maintains the shape of plant cells
beats.explain: Each part does one specialised job, and together they let the plant feed and hold itself up.

beats.prompt: A plant's flowers bloom at the right time of year. What is the plant responding to?

choices.label: The length of the night, through light-sensitive compounds
The ethylene gas it releases
choices.feedback: Ethylene helps control fruit ripening and winter leaf loss, not the timing of blooms.

choices.label: The chlorophyll in its cells
choices.feedback: Chlorophyll lets the plant make nutrients from light; it does not time the blooms.

beats.explain: Light-sensitive compounds respond to the length of the night, a phenomenon called photoperiodism, so many flowering plants bloom at the appropriate time.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Plants need carbon and nitrogen in large quantities.
These are called macronutrients, where macro refers to the quantity needed.
Micronutrients are called that because their particles are tiny.
Micronutrients are required only in trace amounts.
beats.explain: The prefix describes the quantity a plant needs, not the size of the particles, so micro means trace amounts needed.
